This document represents the central component of my habilitation thesis, shortly to be formally submitted. It offers an autonomous overview of my original contributions, including rigorous proofs for each finding. Driven by the need to analyze data residing in Riemannian manifolds, this work aims to develop general, meaningful, and applicable tools for modeling and learning from "Riemannian data." Additionally, it examines the various algorithms involved in such pursuits, including optimization, sampling, and stochastic approximation. The distinct properties of algorithms and data on Riemannian manifolds, compared to their Euclidean equivalents, introduce specific mathematical challenges that this thesis addresses. The initial chapter introduces specialized geometric constructions for use throughout the thesis, while the remaining four chapters tackle series of unresolved problems identified in recent literature. For guidance on navigating the thesis, a one-page introductory guide appears immediately following the table of contents.

The spectral slope of MHD turbulence shifts based on the underlying theoretical framework: KID theory yields a slope of -3/2, whereas Marsch-Matthaeus-Zhou's and Goldreich-Sridhar (often referred to as K-41 like) theories produce -5/3. Other approaches, such as Biskamp's, describe spectra combining both -5/3 and -3/2 regimes. Establishing rigorous mathematical proofs for any of these spectral predictions holds significant scientific value. Building upon the 2012 study by A. Biryuk and W. Craig, we rigorously determine inertial range bounds for the "-5/3" K-like mode in MHD turbulence, explicitly defining the minimum and maximum wave numbers for this power-law scaling. Additionally, we demonstrate that Leray weak solutions of the standard MHD model are bounded in Fourier space with a total spectral energy that is itself time-invariantly bounded; importantly, the average of this system's spectral energy declines over time.

Operators displaying zero-dimensional spectral measures arise inherently within the framework of ergodic Schrödinger operators. We introduce the notion of a complete family of Hausdorff measure functions to examine and differentiate these measures with high precision. We demonstrate that for half-line operators where the positive upper Lyapunov exponent holds for every boundary phase, the dimension of their spectral measures reaches at most logarithmic levels, noting that this limit is sharp through a constructed operator achieving this exact dimension. Additionally, we generalize and enhance fundamental results concerning rank one perturbations and quantum dynamics to include generalized Hausdorff dimensions.

This study explores fluctuations and dissipative behavior within a deformable anti-de Sitter space at high temperature and finite density, where the spacetime geometry corresponds to a charged black hole arising from Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton dynamics. Incorporating horizon function backreaction due to the exponential space deformation, we compute the admittance while analyzing the impacts of temperature and chemical potential. Furthermore, by deriving two-point correlation functions and mean square displacements for both bosons and fermions, we extract short- and long-time asymptotic limits; notably, the long-time regime exhibits sub-diffusion proportional to the logarithm of time. Finally, integrating admittance results with correlation data allows for a verification of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem in systems containing both bosons and fermions.

This paper establishes the concept of weak sharp minima (WSM) within the context of convex interval-valued functions (IVFs). To characterize these minima, the article offers both primal and dual descriptions. The primal characterization utilizes $gH$-directional derivatives. Conversely, the dual characterizations are developed by introducing the support function for subsets of $I(\mathbb{R})^{n}$ and defining $gH$-subdifferentiability for convex IVFs. Furthermore, the work constructs the essential $gH$-subdifferential calculus required for convex IVFs to facilitate these findings. Ultimately, by leveraging this newly developed calculus, the paper delivers dual characterizations for the sets of WSM of such functions.

Multi-modality yields valuable complementary data for clinical prediction, yet missing entries within clinical cohorts restrict the applicability of such approaches to multi-modal learning. Existing imputation strategies often fail to address scenarios where missing data spans heterogeneous modalities (e.g., image versus non-image) or when a single modality is substantially absent. To tackle this, the paper presents a novel method called C-PBiGAN, designed to impute missing information by modeling the joint distribution of multi-modality inputs and building upon the partial bidirectional generative adversarial net (PBiGAN). C-PbiGAN utilizes a conditional latent space within a multi-modal imputation framework; by incorporating available data and enforcing class-regularization losses on reconstructed outputs, the model recovers discriminative details while leveraging conditional signals from existing modalities. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first instance of a generative adversarial framework solving multi-modal imputation through joint modeling of image and non-image data. Validation using both the national lung screening trial (NLST) dataset and an independent external cohort confirms that the C-PBiGAN model significantly improves lung cancer risk assessment compared to standard imputation methods, evidenced by statistically significant increases in AUC metrics relative to the baseline PBiGAN in both the NLST (+2.9%) and proprietary datasets (+4.3%); p<0.05).

Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) serves as a robust method for creating entanglement and typically requires pumping a nonlinear crystal with a fully coherent laser beam. In this study, we overcome this constraint by utilizing commercial light-emitting diode (LED) sources for the pump, despite the counterintuitive nature of the process. Ordinary LEDs possess very low spatial coherence; however, this incoherence is mapped onto the resulting biphoton wavefunction. The type-II phase-matching condition inherently acts as a filter, allowing only specific wavelengths of the LED light to undergo down-conversion and produce localized polarization Bell states, effectively ignoring the lack of global coherence across the transverse plane. Within the standard framework used to demonstrate Bell inequality violations, our experimental analysis of the LEDs' contribution revealed a value of $S=2.33\pm 0.097$, which decisively exceeds the classical limit of $S=2$. This outcome confirms the generation of genuine quantum entanglement. Furthermore, this approach using LEDs can be generalized to other sources of natural light, including sunlight and bioluminescence. Such advancements provide a potential pathway for quantum communication in deep-space missions using light sources that operate without electricity.

Chung-Ang University and Korea University's (CAU_KU) technical report introduces their submission for Track 1, low-quality fake audio detection, at the Audio Deep Synthesis Detection (ADD) 2022 Challenge. To address the challenges posed by poor audio quality, Team proposed frequency feature masking (FFM), an augmentation method verified to be applicable alongside spectrogram-based approaches. This technique, combined with mixup data augmentation, was integrated into five high-performing deep neural networks utilizing mel-spectrogram and constant-Q transform (CQT) for spoofing detection. Ultimately, this approach culminated in their best ranking for Track 1, achieving an Equal Error Rate (EER) of 23.8% to take third place overall.

Theories regarding the spontaneous collapse of the wavefunction attempt to explain why macroscopic systems might violate the laws of quantum mechanics. Yet, conclusive experimental validation has failed so far because detecting the predicted collapse signals above background noise is extremely difficult. In this work, we propose to overcome this limitation by using a superconducting qubit to accurately detect heating effects in a mechanical resonator caused by wavefunction collapse. We demonstrate that strong coupling between the qubit and resonator allows for both rapid measurements and efficient qubit initialization near the ground state; combined, these factors drastically suppress the impact of quasiparticle heating, a noise source predicted to be the most dominant. Furthermore, our findings suggest that bulk acoustic wave resonances could magnify collapse-induced heating by virtue of their exceptionally low dissipation. Collectively, these approaches may pave the way for a definitive test of collapse models.

This study examines the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks applied to determining the ground state of the Schr\"odinger operator within a $d$-dimensional hypercube framework. Under the assumption that the ground state belongs to a spectral Barron space, the authors establish that the convergence of the generalization error remains decaying independently of the dimension $d$. The validity of this assumption is confirmed by deriving a novel regularity estimate for the ground state within this specific space, utilizing a fixed-point method grounded in the Krein-Rutman theorem to achieve the proof.

Cyclotron Radiation Emission Spectroscopy (CRES) represents an increasingly precise methodology for measuring the energies of charged particles through rigorous frequency analysis of the cyclotron radiation they emit. We formalize the signaling dynamics, including noise, for gas-filled fiducial CRES experiments through Hidden Markov models introduced. We developed a novel Hidden Markov model for CRES experiments involving gas within the fiducial volume to characterize signal-noise interactions. We present the innovative use of the Viterbi algorithm to obtain informational thresholds for optimally recognizing cyclotron radiation cues across this class of experiments. Consequently, these experiments provide specific bounds to guide the creation of future reconstruction strategies and detector development. The reliability and consistency of these rules are confirmed via projections and Monte Carlo methods. The robustness of the resulting decision logic is validated with data from Project 8 simulations alongside Monte Carlo realizations. We also employ extensive simulation results backed by experimental inputs.

Utilizing both probability techniques and analytical methods within potential theory, this study examines Dirichlet problems linked to the Dunkl Laplacian $\Delta_k$. Provided certain conditions apply to a bounded domain $D\subset\R^d$ with a continuous boundary function $f$, we demonstrate that a unique solution exists: a continuous function $h$ on the closure of $D$ that is $C^2$ in $D$, satisfies $\Delta_kh=0$ inside $D$, and meets the boundary condition $h=f$. Additionally, a probabilistic representation is presented to describe the unique solution.

We propose exploration potential, a metric assessing the extent to which a reinforcement learning agent investigates dimensions within its class of environments. Unlike information gain, this metric incorporates the task's reward architecture. Consequently, this results in an exploration criterion that is both essential and necessary for achieving asymptotic optimality (acting optimally across all environments in the given class). Through experiments with multi-armed bandits leveraging exploration potential, we examine how various strategies balance the tension between exploration and exploitation.

Advanced battery management systems function as the brain for lithium-ion batteries, demanding models that deliver both speed and precision. Currently, widely used electrochemical and equivalent circuit models fail to fully address this requirement, typically struggling with either computational complexity or predictive accuracy. The situation has become pressing as new battery applications like electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, which operate across wide current ranges, lack viable modeling options in existing literature. To address this gap, we present an innovative model named BattX. BattX utilizes a multi-circuit structure inspired by single particle models that incorporate electrolyte thermal dynamics, effectively blending physical interpretability, computational efficiency, and accuracy. By employing several circuits to emulate key charging and discharge phenomena, and applying a multifaceted experimental strategy to group-wise parameter identification from data, validated tests confirm that BattX accurately predicts voltages from low to high C-rates throughout its operational cycles.

In high energy physics (HEP), particle collisions at facilities like the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) frequently produce jets, defined as correlated clusters of particles. While machine learning (ML) based generative models, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), offer significant promise for speeding up LHC jet simulations, no such models currently exist that utilize jets' native representation as a particle cloud (a set of particles in momentum space) of data. This study introduces JetNet, a new particle cloud dataset, to which established point cloud GANs are applied; the results are assessed using 1-Wasserstein distances between feature distributions, a newly created Fr\'{e}chet ParticleNet Distance, as well as coverage and minimum matching distance metrics. Our findings indicate that existing GANs are insufficient for physics applications, necessitating the development of a new Message Passing GAN (MPGAN). This MPGAN surpasses standard point cloud GANs on nearly all metrics, demonstrating strong potential for HEP use. We posit JetNet as an innovative benchmark for the machine learning community and set MPGAN as the new standard against which future generative models should be improved. To enhance accessibility, reproducibility, and facilitate further research in this domain, we have released an open-source JetNet Python package containing interfaces for particle cloud datasets, evaluation tools, loss metric implementations, and other resources to advance machine learning applications in high energy physics.

Resource-constrained networked autonomous systems must balance efficient task execution with effective resource preservation, though prioritizing conservation often degrades performance. This study specifically tackles the challenge of devising strategies to handle measurement communication costs among agents. While event triggering (ET)—sending measurements only when necessary, such as when Kalman filter innovations surpass a set threshold—is a recognized method for balancing communication overhead with estimation accuracy, agents lack guarantees on task performance when relying solely on implicit information instead of continuous explicit data, a common alternative. We address this gap by introducing a new belief space discretization approach to transform continuous state models into a discrete Markov decision process optimized for ET estimation, effectively managing estimator errors. Utilizing established tools for probabilistic trade-off analysis, we identify the full spectrum of optimal balances between resource usage and task success. From these results, we derive a strategy for selecting ET thresholds. Simualtion outcomes demonstrate that this method efficiently reveals significant trade-offs between performance and energy efficiency with minimal computational cost.

Inferring galaxy attenuation curves is frequently achieved through spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling, in which dust properties are fitted alongside other physical galaxy characteristics. This paper evaluates how effectively SED modeling can derive these curves from broadband data and proposes a novel, flexible model that significantly enhances the accuracy of attenuation curve determination. By fitting simulated spectra generated from the Simba cosmological model with the Prospector code, we investigate this approach. While acknowledging the commonly assumed uniform screen geometry, we introduce a new non-uniform screen model defined by the proportion of unobscured stellar light. This approach permits a fraction of starlight to pass unattenuated, creating a more flexible curve by decoupling UV and optical attenuation profiles. Adopting the non-uniform screen model substantially improves the constraints on the attenuation curve: the median offset in UV attenuation shifts from -0.30 dex under a uniform screen assumption to -0.17 dex with the non-uniform approach. Additionally, the enhanced dust modeling accuracy reduces the average offset in derived star formation rates by 0.12 dex. Finally, we examine the effectiveness of this model, addressing limitations related to stellar-dust geometries and the limits imposed by available observational data.

Electron beam ion sources (EBISs) generate highly charged ions by operating on the principle of electron impact ionization. Besides offering DC ion beams, these systems can produce ion pulses with varying temporal structures. Unlike many other standard ion sources, EBISs provide ion beams characterized by superior beam emission qualities and minimal energy spread. In addition, they act as prolific photon emitters, producing radiation ranging from X-rays through ultraviolet, extreme ultraviolet, to visible light via transitions in highly charged ions. This chapter presents a comprehensive overview encompassing EBIS physical principles, operational methods, and established technical implementations. Through illustrative examples, the text evaluates EBIS performance and highlights their diverse applications across basic research, technological development, and medicine.

We present classical algorithmic methods inspired by quantum amplitude amplification, applied to the $k$-SAT problem, contributing to the growing domain of quantum-inspired classical algorithms. To propose this modification to the Universal SAT (UniSAT) model of $k$-SAT, we treat Boolean satisfiability as finding a global minimum of a non-convex function within a continuous, real-valued context. Our key addition involves applying a conditioning function to the objective, thereby enhancing the values at optimal solution points in a manner analogous to quantum amplification. This technique leads to our proposed method, "AmplifySAT," which operates via a two-phase procedure: an oracle-based lookup followed by a reflection about the current average. Consequently, we evaluate the potential for realizing AmplifySAT within both classical analog and digital computing frameworks and compare it to current approaches in non-convex optimization, such as simulated annealing and gradient descent.

Research area ontologies have demonstrated significant utility in interpreting and analyzing scholarly datasets. This chapter introduces the Computer Science Ontology (CSO), representing the most extensive ontology of computer science domains available, along with various applications founded on CSO. These applications facilitate high-level functions such as topic categorization, metadata retrieval, and book recommendation.

Conducting differential conductance spectroscopy in the high bias regime, where the applied voltage surpasses the sample's work function, fails to reliably approximate the local density of states (LDOS) because the tunnel barrier changes dynamically. Moreover, the significant voltage often renders experiments at constant height difficult, leading researchers to favor constant-current spectroscopy; however, this shift introduces further inaccuracies relative to the true LDOS due to unintended tip-height variations. We introduce a novel normalization framework designed to extract the LDOS from such high-bias scans, applicable in both constant-current and constant-height configurations. This model is expanded to incorporate the influence of in-plane momentum of the probed electronic states on the total current. The effectiveness of this approach is validated by analyzing laterally confined field-emission resonances, which manifest as distinct, peak-like spectroscopic signals characterized by a precise in-plane momentum.

Recent studies have achieved significant success in neural style transfer, but most methods limit stylization to the pixel domain, an approach deemed imperfect as real paintings are composed of brushstrokes rather than pixels. This work argues for a more natural representation where image stylization optimizes parametric brushstrokes instead of pixels. This is accomplished through the introduction of a lightweight differentiable rendering engine that enhances visual fidelity. Furthermore, it grants users additional creative control, allowing manipulation of brushstroke paths. Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative analyses confirm that our parametric framework effectively addresses existing limitations.

Affective polarization, characterized by citizens' intense aversion to opposing party members and their policies, has grown significantly across various democracies. Key drivers include economic strain, widening social gaps, and racial or group-based conflicts, especially when these identities align with established party divides. This paper employs a cultural evolution model to explore how economic forces, inequality, and social dynamics generate and sustain such animosity. The findings indicate that economic downturns not only increase affective polarization and the sorting of racial groups along partisan lines but also intensify existing inter-group inequalities. However, the study offers an optimistic counterpoint: substantial wealth redistribution, facilitated by robust public goods provision, can disrupt this feedback loop and curb polarizing trends. These theoretical conclusions are validated through an analysis of U.S. survey data regarding inter-group relations, racial sorting, and affective polarization over the last fifty years.

We present the Oracle-MNIST dataset, a collection of 28$\times $28 grayscale images featuring 30,222 ancient characters across 10 categories, specifically designed for benchmarking pattern classification tasks that emphasize challenges related to image noise and distortion. The training subset includes 27,222 images, while the test subset contains 300 images per class. Oracle-MNIST utilizes the identical format as the original MNIST dataset, ensuring seamless compatibility with all current classification algorithms and systems, yet it presents a considerably more difficult classification problem. These ancient character images exhibit two key characteristics essential for machine learning research: (1) severe and distinct noises resulting from three decades of burial and aging, and (2) highly varied traditional writing styles by ancient Chinese calligraphy. The dataset is available for free at https://github.com/wm-bupt/oracle-mnist.

We introduce Typography-MNIST (TMNIST), a dataset containing 565,292 grayscale images, structured similarly to standard MNIST data. These images cover 1,812 distinct glyphs drawn from varied styles available across 1,355 Google Fonts. Among the glyphs are over 150 modern and historical language scripts and symbols, organized into distinct font-style subsets. This data product was created as part of the CognitiveType project, which seeks to develop eye-tracking methodologies for mapping type real-time and establishing computational tools for designing typefaces with enhanced cognitive attributes like readability. Both the dataset and the accompanying script code for generating font-specific glyphs are available open-source via GitHub under the repository CognitiveType (https://github.com/aiskunks/CognitiveType).

Given that prompt diagnosis and treatment are the most critical aspects of managing cerebral palsy (CP), developing a highly efficient and interpretable automated prediction system is vital. This study highlights a notable distinction between the human movement frequencies of infants diagnosed with CP and those of healthy children, an insight that enhances prediction accuracy yet remains underutilized in most current deep learning-based CP prediction models. This paper introduces a Frequency Attention-Informed Graph Convolutional Network (FA-GNN), which is evaluated using two consumer-level RGB video datasets: MINI-RGBD and RVI-38. The proposed frequency attention module not only boosts classification performance but also improves the system's interpretability. Furthermore, we implemented a frequency-binning technique that preserves essential frequency data regarding human joint positions while eliminating noise. The results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on both datasets. This research confirms that incorporating frequency information can non-intrusively aid in predicting CP, offering a practical approach for early diagnostics in areas with limited clinical resources.

With the global shift toward data-driven sectors, there is surging demand for automated algorithms that can transform scanned digital documents into machine-readable content. This technology not only facilitates data digitization for advanced analytics but also substantially automates workflows previously reliant on manual review. While optical character recognition has effectively addressed text extraction from images over the years, extracting table semantics has historically received less attention. Table recognition comprises two primary challenges: detection and structure recognition. Most existing research focuses on just one of these tasks, often neglecting fully end-to-end solutions or the complexities of real-world document conditions, such as rotated images or noise. Consequently, recent research increasingly relies on deep learning combined with transfer learning for structure recognition, driven by the scarcity of large-scale datasets. This paper introduces "Multi-Type-TD-TSR," a multi-stage pipeline providing a comprehensive end-to-end solution. It employs state-of-the-art deep learning models for detection and distinguishes among three table categories based on bordering styles. For structure recognition, it applies a deterministic, non-data-driven algorithm applicable across all table types, which is itself founded on two specific algorithms tailored for unbordered and bordered tables respectively. Evaluated on the ICDAR 2019 table structure recognition dataset, Multi-Type-TD-TSR establishes a new state-of-the-art performance level.

Knowledge Graphs like DBpedia and Freebase often suffer from incomplete entity type information, stemming from both automated processes and manual curation constraints. Entity type inference is a critical procedure for assigning or determining these semantic types within such graphs. This paper introduces *GRAND*, an innovative method for entity type inference that combines textual descriptions with various graph walk strategies employed by RDF2vec, which first generates random walks and subsequently utilizes a language model to derive node embeddings. This research highlights how the specific strategy for generating walks and the choice of embedding model substantially influence performance on entity type inference. Additionally, *GRAND* achieves superior performance compared to baselines on the standard benchmarks (FIGER and DBpedia) for classifying entities across both coarse and fine categories. Optimal results were obtained by leveraging order-sensitive RDF2walk variants alongside contextual embeddings derived from textual descriptions of entities.

Do-calculus focuses on estimating interventional probabilities based on observed joint distributions within a specific causal framework. While these rules allow for the derivation of all identifiable causal effects, they do not inherently indicate whether an effect is identifiable or not. Shpitser and Pearl developed an algorithm specifically for this determination in causal models with unobserved variables, represented as directed acyclic graphs. This algorithm, which applies do-calculus rules and probability properties iteratively, successfully produces an expression for the causal distribution if the effect is identifiable, or concludes the effect is non-identifiable if derivation fails. This paper presents the R package *causaleffect*, which implements the aforementioned algorithm and demonstrates its capabilities through illustrative examples.

This paper presents a framework utilizing differential dynamic programming (DDP) to generate polynomial trajectories for differentially flat systems. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on linear equations growing in size with the number of polynomial segments—common in existing literature—we adopt a state-space perspective. In this approach, the system's size remains constant, reducing the problem to a finite horizon control setting where continuity across adjacent polynomials is automatically enforced. As a result, constraint optimization for trajectory generation, whether time-optimized or not, is transformed into a discrete-time finite-horizon optimal control problem with inequality constraints. This formulation is solved using a specialized interior-point DDP (IPDDP) algorithm. Additionally, for a specific case of unconstrained generation with preallocated time, we demonstrate the problem reduces linearly-quadratic (LQT), corresponding to an exact DDP iteration in a single step. All discussed algorithms scale linearly with the number of trajectory segments. Numerical experiments against current best practices and real-world physical tests are included to confirm and validate these theoretical results. Furthermore, implementation code will be made available open source.

Cosmic rays (CRs) are believed to play a significant role as feedback agents in star-forming galaxies, capable of providing pressure support and potentially driving galactic winds. Utilizing multidimensional CR-magnetohydrodynamic simulations that incorporate streaming and diffusive transport, we examined the launching of winds from an initially static atmosphere driven solely by CRs. By comparing our estimated CR-metric Eddington limit—where CR force supersedes gravity—to modeled systems, we scaled these findings to star-forming contexts. Our analysis suggests that CRs can contribute to outflow dynamics across a wide spectrum of star formation environments. Furthermore, we calculated the energy and momentum exchange between the gas and CRs, as well as mass outflow rates, while accounting for varying degrees of influence attributed to streaming versus diffusion. Simulations featuring streaming revealed the emergence and saturation of CR acoustic instability; however, CRs and gas remained tightly coupled, allowing efficient momentum transfer even amid the instability. Increased CR fluxes resulted in greater thermal energy deposition and more vigorous outflows. specifically, when streaming occurs, the majority of transferred energy manifests as Alfvénon wave heating, raising gas pressure and internal energy, while only a fraction converts into outflow kinetic energy. Additionally, we explored scenarios with radiative cooling, which altered gas temperature and pressure distributions but appeared to have minimal impact on mass outflow rates when CR fluxes surpassed the super-Eddington limit.

By integrating the Halperin-Mazenco formalism with Gross-Pitaevskii theory, we analyze the kinematics and nucleation of quantum vortices in two-dimensional stirred Bose Einstein condensates. This study defines the disorder field, representing the topologically conserved vorticity of a smooth superfluid. By utilizing this field along with its associated current density to examine precursor patterns emerging within the oscillating potential, we identify how specific conditions lead to the creation and expulsion of vortices. Our results indicate that while phase slips occur freely inside hard potential wells without spontaneous nucleation, soft potential wells only exhibit this phenomenon once the stirring surpasses a critical threshold that triggers vortex nucleation. Furthermore, the Halperin-Mazenco framework serves as a refined and elegant approach for extracting the full dynamics of the point vortex system directly from the Gross-Pitaevskii equation.

This study examines the resolution of inverse eigenvalue problems using machine learning techniques, specifically focusing on two scenarios: inverting Sturm-Liouville eigenvalues for symmetric potentials and inverting transmission eigenvalues for spherically symmetric refractive indices. Initially, direct problems are addressed to generate necessary eigenvalue datasets, enabling the training of learning algorithms. Subsequently, various inverse problems are investigated, and the efficacy of different models in reconstructing the specific potentials or refractive indices from limited sets of low-order eigenvalues is evaluated. The employed supervised regression models include k-Nearest Neighbours, Random Forests, and Multi-Layer Perceptrons. Experimental results confirm that, with suitable parameter optimization, these machine learning approaches can successfully solve the studied inverse eigenvalue tasks numerically.

Individuals react varyingly to inspirations presented during brainstorming sessions. Previous studies on extensive ideation systems have explored this phenomenon via timing, inspiration similarity, and integration but overlooked individual preferences. To address this gap, our research focuses specifically on user preferences regarding inspiration. In long capillaries where $a<2/\pi$, condensation follows type I behavior, featuring pinned menisci at the top edges with defined contact angles. Capillaries of intermediate length, satisfying $2/\pi<a<1$, may display either type I behavior (with fixed angles) or type II behavior (characterized by overspill reservoirs and no pinning), the outcome depending specifically on the contact angle. Conversely, short capillaries where $a>1$ consistently exhibit type II condensation regardless of other parameters. Across all regimes, capillary condensation vanishes completely if contact angles exceed a critical threshold. We identify a distinct, continuous phase transition within the liquid-like condensed phase linked to the depinning and rounding of menisci around the slit's upper edges. To quantify this, we derive finite-size scaling predictions that connect the transitions between phase boundaries grounded in wetting and filling fluctuation theories. Finally, we utilize fully microscopic Density Functional Theory simulations to rigorously test these predictions and validate the molecular-scale mechanisms governing both forms of capillary condensation and their suppression.

This work introduces novel differential privacy frameworks specifically designed for data products subject to simultaneous \emph{invariant} maintenance and strict \emph{integer} constraints. Such requirements are critical in real-world private data curation tasks, exemplified by the release of the 2020 U.S. Decennial Census, yet they significantly complicate the creation of data products that offer adequate statistical utility alongside provable privacy guarantees. We introduce the concept of \emph{integer subspace differential privacy} to precisely formalize the assurance provided to these constrained outputs and establish the composition and post-processing properties inherent to our approach. To overcome the difficulties associated with sampling from highly restricted discrete domains defined by these constraints, we develop a pair of unbiased additive sampling mechanisms—named the generalized Laplace and generalized Gaussian mechanisms—derived through solutions to the governing Diophantine equations. The resulting mechanisms ensure high accuracy, characterized by error distributions featuring sub-exponential tail behaviors for the former and sub-Gaussian tails for the latter. For practical implementation, we design an MCMC algorithm and provide an empirical convergence assessment by analyzing estimated upper bounds on total variation distance via $L$-lag coupling techniques. The effectiveness of our methodology is validated through several case studies, including synthetic scenarios with intersecting invariants, the publication of a sensitive contingency table with fixed margins, and an application to the 2010 Census data employing mandatory state-level population totals.

Categories such as plants or furniture are acquired in early childhood and serve a crucial function in how individuals process, organize, and share their understanding of the world. Although these categories and their definitions are consistent across different cultures, enabling an efficient encoding of worldly complexity, current models of category learning and representation are mostly evaluated using small-scale, controlled studies. Furthermore, experimental participation is typically limited to individuals from specific cultural and socioeconomic background, predominantly English-speaking Westerners like U.S. undergraduates. This research examines whether categorization models generalize when faced with large, complex, and noisy datasets reminiscent of the human environment and when applied across different languages and cultures. We introduce a Bayesian cognitive model that can discover structured category representations from natural language data, allowing for the test of these models on expansive scales and their application to a diverse range of languages. Our findings demonstrate that meaningful, large-scale conceptual categories emerge universally. This project highlights the utility of combining recent computational modeling techniques with large naturalistic datasets for cognitive science inquiries.

In condensed-matter physics, electronic Mott insulators have been a significant area of study given their deep connection to high-temperature superconductivity. In contrast to atomic systems—where Mott phases have been recently demonstrated for particles including electrons, protons (fermions), and atoms (bosons)—a Mott state defined by bosons has yet to be detected in the solid state. Our work uncovers this missing signature by utilizing a Bose-Jay Cummings-type interaction of bosons via semiconductor excitons trapped within artificial two-dimensional lattices. Our focus is on the regime where local interaction strength rivals the confinement energy levels. In this setting, we find that Mott localization of one or more excitons (two-body states max) per lattice site can readily occur. Furthermore, our platform allows custom design (on-demand programming) regarding lattice site structure and geometry, which together with strong dipolar interactions and Bose condensation in two-dimensional space will offer a fresh avenue for exploring many-body physics with spontaneously symmetry broken phases.

This study examines exclusive $\pi^-\Delta^{++}$ electroproduction using the handbag framework, where helicity amplitudes decompose into hard subprocesses and generalized parton distributions (GPDs). We establish the $p\text{-}\Delta$ GPDs corresponding to transverse spin configurations, adopting known non-flip GPDs from existing work. To estimate observable magnitudes, we rely on large-$N_C$ constraints to link selected $p\text{-}\Delta$ GPDs to their proton-to-proton counterparts while suppressing the remaining contributions. Our calculation of twist-2 and twist-3 hard subprocess amplitudes incorporates quark transverse momentum effects alongside Sudakov factor suppression, thereby predicting partial cross sections for $\gamma^*p\to \pi^-\Delta^{++}$ within the large-$N_C$ approximation.

Quantum walks serve as potent resources for constructing search and sampling algorithms, specifically for generating quantum stationary states. However, the success probabilities of these methods typically fall significantly short of 1. While amplitude amplification can boost success rates, it introduces the "soufflé" phenomenon; the optimal timing must be precise because the probability peaks at the ideal step count but diminishes if additional steps are applied without knowledge of this optimum. This uncertainty complicates real-world algorithmic deployment. This work introduces generalized interpolated quantum walks, which simultaneously enhance the success probability of search procedures and circumvent the souffle issue. By combining these walks with quantum fast-forwarding, we reduce the query complexity for the search walk operator significantly—to $\Theta(\log(\varepsilon^{-1})\sqrt{\Heg})$ from $\Theta((\varepsilon^{-1})\sqrt{\Heg})$—and lower the required number of ancilla qubits to $\Theta(\log\log(\varepsilon^{-1})+\log\sqrt{\Heg})$ from $\Theta(\log(\varepsilon^{-1})+\log\sqrt{\Heg})$. In doing so, we avoid the souffle problem and improve success rates. Additionally, we demonstrate their effectiveness in improving the construction of quantum stationary distributions. Finally, by applying our methodology, we provide a mechanism to build sequential, slowly evolving Markov chains, a requisite precursor for preparing adiabatic stationary states.

This work employs the functional renormalization group to analyze a $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric gauge theory comprising a quiral superfield coupled to a vector $U(1)$ superfield. We establish that the nonrenormalization theorem remains valid at the leading order of the supercovariant derivative expansion. Furthermore, we calculate the beta functions and investigate fixed point behaviors under a local potential assumption, with a discussion of the regulators used.

The lattice size $\operatorname{ls_\Delta}(P)$ of a lattice polytope $P$ serves as a crucial invariant; originally defined in the context of bounding the total degree and bi-degree of equations defining algebraic curves, the concept has long been present implicitly within geometric combinatorics. This paper demonstrates that for any empty lattice polytope $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ contained in $\mathbb{Z}^3$ space, there exists a specific basis that calculates the lattice size $\operatorname{ls_\Delta}(P)$. This finding enables a swift algorithm for determining this metric. Furthermore, the study expands upon this result to include a separate category of lattice polytopes with a lattice width of one within $\mathbb{R}^3$. The discussion concludes by presenting a counterexample to show that the proposed outcome fails for general lattice polytopes $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ possessing a lattice width of one.

In 2017, Colorado implemented Risk-Limiting Audits (RLAs) throughout the state, employing both ballot-level comparison and ballot-polling techniques. However, these audits were limited to elections confined within a single county, as existing techniques for efficiently auditing multi-jurisdictional contests that integrate both polling and comparison methods are currently unavailable. The existing audit software, RLATool, requires improvements to handle cross-county contests and to process small races more effectively. This paper addresses these gaps by outlining several strategies: simple but inefficient approaches, more efficient methods that utilize stratified sampling to combine polynomial ballot comparisons, and techniques that integrate ballot-level comparison with variable-size batch assessments without relying on stratified sampling. The discussion includes conclusions and illustrative recommendations evaluated through examples that contrast these methods against current practices. Additionally, open-source exemplar code and interactive Jupyter notebooks are provided to implement these methodologies and facilitate further investigation.

Recent advancements in self-supervision have discovered feature representations comparable to those achieved with full supervision, demonstrating benefits in enhancing robustness and out-of-distribution detection. Although self-supervision can enhance robustness, the specifics of implementation are critical. Simply incorporating extra self-supervision losses jointly with adversarial training improves accuracy only for perturbations with magnitudes similar to or smaller than the training value $\epsilon_{test} \leq \epsilon_{pred}$. However, when testing at magnitudes where $\epsilon_{pred} \geq \epsilon_{test}$, model accuracy declines; notably, increasing the weight of the self-supervision loss exacerbates this performance degradation. The study identifies several methods for integrating self-supervision into adversarial training and finds that using self-supervised objectives to optimize both network parameters and generate adversarial examples yields the strongest improvements in robustness, analogous to ensemble adversarial training. Bayesian optimization typically requires "inner optimization" of a non-convex, highly multi-modal acquisition function that often fails local numerical optimizers due to non-differentiability or similar constraints. In response, randomness over discrete candidates frequently replaces continuous searches. We introduce candidate points derived from the Delaunay triangulation of current input designs, detailing their construction. Empirical results on both synthetic benchmarks and real simulations demonstrate that these "trisands," or Delaunay-based candidates, outperform both numerically optimized and random alternatives and are highly adaptable for hybrid frameworks.

Recent years have highlighted advanced quantum control techniques for three-level systems as a pivotal area of inquiry within quantum information science and technology. This work offers numerical simulations derived from pragmatic experimental conditions to assess quantum process tomography in STIRAP and superadiabatic (saSTIRAP). A pivotal step involves establishing a basis in operator space composed of the identity operator and eight Gell-Mann operators, facilitating an analysis of process matrices defined by their 81 constituent elements ($9 \times 9$). Our discussion covers outcomes for both an ideal, decoherence-free scenario and a model reflecting experimental reality that incorporates decoherence.

These results summarize the most recent data from the ATLAS experiment on photon production concurrent with a top-quark pair in proton-proton collisions at the LHC at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The findings detail measurements of both inclusive and differential cross-sections within single-lepton and dilepton final states, calculated for the fiducial volume defined by the detector's acceptance.

We report the detection of a novel cosmological signal known as the Doppler-boosted Cosmic Infrared Background (DB-CIB). This phenomenon originates from the unique motions of the host galaxies generating the thermal dust emission associated with the cosmic infrared background (CIB). As an independent probe of the cosmic velocity field, DB-CIB closely resembles the kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect but offers a critical advantage: it is immune to the kSZ optical depth degeneracy. This immunity stems from the fact that DB-CIB is not sensitive to the intricate astrophysical processes governing galaxy formation. We anticipate that this effect will be observable through cross-correlations between data from CCAT-Prime and DESI-like experiments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that DB-CIB manifests as a new foreground in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) spectrum. Consequentially, if not accurately corrected, this foreground will introduce a bias into future attempts to measure kSZ cross-correlations.

Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes (MMDP) serve as a robust framework for modeling sequential decision-making in cooperative multi-agent scenarios, with numerous algorithms relying on centralized or decentralized planning. Despite this progress, the scalability and efficiency of existing methods are often hampered by rapidly changing environments and the overwhelming size of the combined state and action spaces. While FV-MCTS-MP (centralized) and *Alternate maximization with Behavioural Cloning* (decentralized) have recently demonstrated strong MMDP performance, they fail to effectively adapt to dynamic shifts and address communication limitations among agents, respectively. In response, this work proposes SiCLOP, a simulation-driven online planning algorithm designed for cooperative multi-agent environments. SiCLOP integrates Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with Coordination Graphs (CG) and Graph Neural Networks (GCN) to learn coordinated behavior, delivering real-time MMDP solutions. Through effective pruning of the action space, the algorithm enhances scalability, and it distinguishes itself from prior works by supporting transfer learning, allowing learned agents to deploy across different environments. Furthermore, the study includes a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence within multi-agent contexts and provides extensive empirical evidence demonstrating that SiCLOP significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art online planning methods.

We introduce the 1-100 GeV spectral energy distribution (SED) for 148 recently detected high-synchrotron-peaked blazars (HSPs) from the First Brazil-ICRANet Gamma-ray Blazar catalogue (1BIGB). Many of these sources are new to previous Fermi-LAT catalogues, marking a significant expansion of the known gamma-ray blazar population with previously unpublished spectral properties. Given that the sample was initially selected based on excess signals in the 0.3-500 GeV band, these objects are promising candidates for very-high-energy (VHE) emission that may be detectable by the upcoming CTA observatory. Our flux estimates utilize Passage 8 data spanning over nine years of Fermi-LAT observations. We additionally review the full 0.3-500 GeV broadband fitting from the original 1BIGB study for all sources, refreshing the power-law parameters with the latest dataset and assessing their relevance to current VHE studies and future CTA prospects. To evaluate CTA detectability, we extrapolate the gamma-ray SEDs for a subsample using extragalactic background light correction to compare against CTA sensitivity curves. Detailed analysis is provided for two specific sources, 1BIGB J224910.6-130002 and 1BIGB J194356.2+211821. All newly presented gamma-ray SEDs are openly accessible through the Brazilian Science Data Center (BSDC) at CBPF in Rio de Janeiro.

"End user analysis" denotes the process of deriving physics results from reconstructed and simulated experimental data. This report outlines the work undertaken by the Computational Frontier topical group regarding this domain for Snowmass 2021. Within high energy physics, experimental systems execute common tasks such as simulation, calibration, and reconstruction to generate shared data pools. From these comprehensive samples, diverse analysis datasets are curated—typically tailored for specific physics inquiries through trigger events or data object selection—subsequently examined by analysts to yield physics results. Community consensus led to the classification of the end user analysis landscape into five pillars: analysis models, ecosystem components, data management and formats, collaborative tools, and training resources. We detail findings and recommendations concerning how these critical areas influence end user analysis.
